strengths: The manuscript addresses a real bottleneck in computer vision for materials science: dense instance-level segmentation of electron micrographs. The scale claimed for UniEM-3M, 5,091 high-resolution images and about 3M instance masks, is substantially beyond prior EM segmentation datasets and could be valuable if released in a usable form.

The contribution is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks paper rather than primarily an Algorithms/General paper. Under that lens, the combination of instance masks, structured image-level descriptions, segmentation benchmarks, and a fine-tuned text-to-image model is timely and potentially impactful.

The paper benchmarks a reasonably broad set of segmentation methods, including natural-image instance segmentation models and field/cell-segmentation style methods. The results clearly identify high-density EM segmentation as a challenging setting where standard detection-based instance segmentation is inadequate.

The annotation pipeline is thoughtfully motivated for dense EMs, with a custom web platform, expert review, staged quality control, and supplementary details about prompts and implementation. The dataset statistics and visual examples support the claim that the images contain substantial variation in morphology, density, scale, and microscopy conditions.

The synthetic-data experiments are useful: training with generated data alone and combining generated with real data provide some evidence that the diffusion model captures task-relevant visual structure, not just visually plausible samples.
weaknesses: The biggest concern is reproducibility and benchmark utility: the paper states that only a subset of UniEM-3M will be publicly released, while the benchmark, diffusion model, and main claims are based on the complete collection. Without a clear commitment on exactly what data, labels, splits, metadata, licenses, and evaluation server will be available, the central dataset/benchmark contribution is difficult to verify or use.

Dataset provenance and rights are under-specified. The data come from academic collaborations, web crawling, and Aversa et al.; however, the manuscript does not give enough detail about licensing, consent, redistribution rights, de-duplication against public benchmarks, or whether web-crawled images can legally support a released dataset or trained generative model.

Annotation quality is described procedurally but not quantified. For a dataset paper with 3M instances, I would expect inter-annotator agreement, expert audit statistics, correction rates after pseudo-label refinement, failure-mode analysis, and perhaps a manually verified gold subset. The use of model-assisted pseudo-labels and diffusion-augmented training in the annotation loop raises possible bias issues that are not empirically characterized.

The segmentation benchmark has fairness and completeness issues. Anchor-based methods are only trained/evaluated on the sparse subset because of computational limitations, so Table 2 is not a fully comparable benchmark across the whole dataset. The sparse/dense split threshold of 100 instances is weakly justified, and the main evaluation relies heavily on AP/PQ at IoU 0.5, which may not capture boundary precision needed for scientific measurements.

The proposed UniEM-Net appears largely derived from Cellpose-style flow fields with a SAM-ViT backbone, and the architectural novelty is not explained in enough detail to evaluate independently. Ablations isolating the modified Euler integration, boundary/skeleton features, backbone choice, post-processing, and generated-data augmentation are missing.

The generative-model evaluation is preliminary. FID and DINO-style similarity do not establish prompt controllability, scientific validity, privacy preservation, or absence of memorization. Claims that the model can act as a substitute for sensitive original data need stronger evidence, including nearest-neighbor/memorization analysis and expert validation of generated microstructure realism.

The structured text annotations are potentially interesting but only evaluated indirectly. There is no quantitative assessment of attribute accuracy after Gemini/GPT extraction plus cross-checking, no analysis by attribute, and no downstream vision-language benchmark despite the paper emphasizing multimodal utility.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence supports, especially “universal,” “first large-scale and multimodal,” “privacy-preserving surrogate,” and “state-of-the-art baseline.” The paper would be more convincing with clearer scope boundaries, public release details, and external validation on existing EM datasets or held-out laboratories/instruments.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underserved problem: instance-level segmentation and text-conditioned generation for materials electron micrographs, where dense microstructures and heterogeneous acquisition conditions are genuinely challenging.

As a Datasets/Benchmarks-style contribution, the proposed collection is potentially valuable: 5,091 EM images with roughly 3 million instance labels, structured image-level attributes, and train/test benchmarking would fill a real gap relative to existing EM datasets that are smaller or lack instance annotations.

The manuscript includes a broad set of baseline comparisons across detection-based, anchor-free, star-convex/polygon, and flow/field-based methods, which helps characterize why dense EM scenes are difficult for standard natural-image instance segmentation methods.

The idea of pairing the dataset with a fine-tuned text-to-image model is interesting, especially for augmentation and for partially mitigating restrictions on sharing proprietary or sensitive EM data.
weaknesses: The central dataset contribution is weakened by unclear and apparently incomplete release plans: the paper says only a subset of UniEM-3M will be public, while benchmarks are run on the complete dataset. This makes the benchmark, claimed scale, and model comparisons difficult to reproduce or fairly use by the community.

Dataset provenance, licensing, privacy, and attribution are under-specified. The data come from academic collaborations, web crawling, and a public dataset, but the paper does not clearly document licenses, redistribution rights, crawling criteria, consent/ownership constraints, or what exactly is excluded from release.

Annotation quality is asserted rather than demonstrated. The paper describes expert review and a multi-stage pipeline, but gives no inter-annotator agreement, audit sample accuracy, boundary/mask error statistics, pseudo-label correction rates, or quantitative validation of the 3M instance labels. For a dataset paper, this is a major evidential gap.

The structured text annotations rely heavily on Gemini/GPT plus cross-checking, yet there is no quantitative evaluation of attribute accuracy, consistency, expert correction frequency, or failure modes. The claim of high-fidelity attribute-disentangled descriptions is therefore not well supported.

The UniEM-Net technical contribution appears incremental and close to Cellpose-style flow supervision with a SAM-ViT backbone. The paper lacks sufficient architectural detail, ablations, or analysis to separate gains from backbone choice, training protocol, generated data, and the flow formulation itself.

The experimental comparison is not fully convincing. Several natural-image baselines are only trained/evaluated on the sparse subset because dense inference is difficult, while flow-based methods are evaluated on both sparse and dense data. This may be practically motivated, but it limits the strength of claims about overall superiority.

Some claims overstate the results. In dense scenes, UniEM-Net only slightly exceeds Cellpose-SAM in mAP and is essentially tied in PQ, yet the text claims its superiority is most evident in dense scenarios and qualitatively nearly indistinguishable from ground truth. No variance, statistical testing, or per-category breakdown is provided.

The generative-model evaluation is weak. FID/style similarity and t-SNE overlap against the training distribution do not establish scientific fidelity, controllability, novelty, or privacy preservation. The claim that the diffusion model can act as a proxy for the complete private data distribution is especially strong and not adequately validated.

There is potential circularity and leakage risk in the data engine: generated data are used in the iterative annotation/training workflow, and then generated data are evaluated as augmentation for the same benchmark. The manuscript does not clearly separate train/test sources, generator training data, pseudo-labeling iterations, and benchmark evaluation to rule out leakage.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete despite some implementation notes. The release URL is a placeholder, dataset split definitions are not specified, compute/training schedules are uneven across methods, and there is no clear statement that code, exact prompts, trained weights, and full evaluation scripts will be released.

The work lacks external validation on independent EM datasets or downstream materials-science measurements. Since the paper claims universality and broad materials applicability, evaluation confined to its own partially private dataset is insufficient.

The manuscript has clarity and presentation issues, including imprecise claims such as 'first large-scale and universal,' vague descriptions of web-crawled data and expert validation, and qualitative figures that are too small to substantiate several detailed claims.

strengths: The paper is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, with accompanying baseline and generative-model components. Under that framing, the central contribution is strong: UniEM-3M provides 5,091 high-resolution electron micrographs, about 3M instance labels, and structured image-level text attributes, addressing a real scarcity of large, dense, materials-oriented EM segmentation data.

The dataset appears substantially more challenging and useful than prior EM segmentation resources: it covers diverse materials, morphologies, densities, resolutions, and instance scales, with many high-density scenes that stress standard instance segmentation pipelines.

The annotation pipeline is thoughtfully designed for the domain, including a custom high-density annotation platform, human-in-the-loop pseudo-label refinement, peer review, and expert validation. This is a meaningful practical contribution beyond simply collecting images.

The benchmark is useful and reasonably broad, comparing anchor-based, anchor-free, star-convex/polygonal, and field-based methods. The results clearly demonstrate that dense EM instance segmentation has different failure modes from natural-image segmentation, and that field-based methods are better suited to this setting.

The release of a fine-tuned text-to-image diffusion model, together with experiments showing synthetic data improves downstream segmentation, adds practical value and partially mitigates the fact that the full dataset cannot be released.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with helpful dataset statistics, comparisons to prior resources, implementation details in the supplement, qualitative visualizations, and quantitative segmentation/generation evaluations.
weaknesses: The biggest concern is reproducibility and long-term benchmark value: only a subset of UniEM-3M will be publicly released, while the benchmark results are reported on the complete dataset. This limits independent verification and may reduce the utility of the benchmark unless the public subset, splits, annotations, and evaluation server are very clearly specified.

Dataset provenance and licensing are under-specified. The data come partly from academic/industrial collaborations, automated web crawling, and Aversa et al.; the paper does not sufficiently detail permissions, licenses, de-identification, redistribution rights, or whether crawled images can be included in the public release.

Annotation quality is described procedurally but not quantified. There are no inter-annotator agreement statistics, expert audit pass rates, boundary-quality measurements, or analysis of failure cases in pseudo-label-assisted annotation, which matters for a dataset claiming nearly 3M high-quality instance masks.

The UniEM-Net algorithmic novelty is moderate. It is strongly inspired by Cellpose-style flow fields with a SAM-ViT backbone, and the paper does not provide enough ablations to isolate which parts of the method, training recipe, or synthetic-data augmentation drive the gains.

The benchmark comparison has some fairness and completeness issues. Anchor-based methods are trained/evaluated only on the sparse subset because dense cases are computationally difficult, so the dense comparison is incomplete. Hyperparameter tuning appears limited, and there is no runtime/memory table despite computational scalability being a core claim.

The generative-model evaluation is suggestive but not fully convincing. FID, DINO style similarity, t-SNE plots, and downstream segmentation gains are useful, but attribute controllability, scientific validity, diversity, and possible memorization/privacy leakage are not rigorously evaluated, despite the claim that the generator can act as a privacy-preserving surrogate for unreleased data.

The structured text annotations are potentially valuable, but their correctness is mostly asserted through LLM cross-checking and expert resolution. The paper would be stronger with a held-out expert evaluation of attribute accuracy and an analysis of ambiguous categories such as material type, morphology, and layering.

strengths: The paper introduces a substantial Datasets/Benchmarks contribution for materials electron microscopy: 5,091 raw EM images with about 3 million instance masks, structured image-level attributes, and SEM/TEM coverage. The scale and density of instance annotation appear meaningfully beyond prior public EM segmentation datasets, and the dataset targets a real gap for dense microstructural analysis.

The annotation pipeline is thoughtfully described, with model-assisted labeling, peer review, expert final validation, and a 300-image independently reannotated subset. Reporting Krippendorff's alpha and PQ across pseudo-label, peer-review, and final-validation stages provides useful evidence that the labels are not merely unchecked model outputs.

The benchmark is broad and practically informative. It compares detection-based, query-based, and bottom-up instance segmentation methods, and the results clearly show why dense EM images stress standard natural-image instance segmentation pipelines.

The accompanying UniAIMS baseline is not claimed as a fundamentally new architecture, which is appropriate for this contribution type. As an EM-tailored flow-based baseline, it gives the benchmark a strong reference point and exposes remaining headroom, especially via the PQ@90 drop and the gap to human agreement.

The synthetic-data component is useful rather than decorative: the authors fine-tune SDXL with structured prompts, evaluate generated images with distributional metrics, and show downstream gains from generated data and generated-data pretraining.
weaknesses: The manuscript would benefit from stronger reproducibility details around the dataset release. The paper states that the dataset, generation model, and demo are publicly available, but the manuscript shown here leaves the links blank/anonymized and does not clearly specify license terms, permissible use, or long-term hosting details.

Data provenance and rights are under-specified for a dataset paper. About 10% of images come from web crawling and 6% from a public dataset; the paper should more clearly state filtering criteria, copyright/licensing checks, redistribution permissions, and how industrial/academic collaboration data can be released.

The structured text annotations rely heavily on GPT/Gemini plus expert review, but the paper gives limited quantitative validation of attribute correctness beyond consistency workflow descriptions. Attribute-label accuracy, ambiguity rates, and per-attribute correction statistics would strengthen the multimodal claim.

The comparison to top-down and query-based methods is informative but not fully satisfying: those methods are evaluated only on the sparse subset, largely with default detection limits. This is reasonable as a practical baseline, but it weakens claims about their intrinsic unsuitability unless accompanied by tuned high-query/high-detection variants or more controlled scaling experiments.

The generative evaluation is promising but still somewhat indirect. FID/style scores and downstream segmentation gains support utility, yet there is limited expert assessment of physical plausibility, failure modes, or whether recombined attributes can create scientifically misleading microstructures.

Several important implementation details are pushed to the supplement or described at a high level, including UniAIMS modifications, data sanitation, annotation tooling, and synthetic mask generation/usage. For a benchmark intended to seed future work, clearer main-paper details on exact splits, preprocessing, prompts, and evaluation scripts would improve reproducibility.

The dataset distribution is long-tailed and heavily SEM-dominated, with limited evidence that minority modalities/material classes are adequately represented for robust multimodal or cross-instrument conclusions. The paper acknowledges diversity, but more stratified performance analysis would clarify where the benchmark is strongest and weakest.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underserved problem: dense instance segmentation for materials electron micrographs, where public large-scale expert-labeled data are genuinely scarce.

If released as described, EM3M would be a useful resource: 5,091 EM images, about 3M instance masks, structured image-level attributes, and benchmarks across several segmentation paradigms represent a potentially meaningful dataset/benchmark contribution.

The manuscript includes some useful dataset characterization, including instance-count and area distributions, attribute distributions, and an inter-annotator study on a stratified subset of 300 images.
The open-problems section is unusually candid about remaining difficulty, especially the large drop at stricter PQ@90 and the gap between model performance and human agreement.
weaknesses: The main contribution is best assessed as Datasets/Benchmarks rather than Algorithms/General, since UniAIMS is explicitly an implementation-level adaptation of Cellpose rather than a new architecture. Under that lens, the dataset could be valuable, but the paper does not provide enough confidence in provenance, licensing, release terms, or reproducibility. The dataset, generation, and demo footnotes are blank in the manuscript, and there is no clear license or access plan.

Data provenance is under-specified and potentially problematic. Around 10% of images are from automated web crawling, but the paper does not explain source filtering, permissions, copyright/license compatibility, consent from academic/industrial collaborators, or whether proprietary metadata were removed. This is a major issue for a dataset paper.

The annotation protocol is not described with enough operational detail to support the claimed label quality. The authors rely on pseudo-labels from a model trained with synthetic augmentation, followed by refinement, but do not report how much manual correction was needed, annotator training, time/cost, failure cases, or quality statistics beyond the 300-image subset. The reported final-validation PQ of 0.784 is close to human agreement but still leaves substantial uncertainty for 3M masks.

The benchmark protocol is not fully convincing. Detection/query methods are evaluated only on a sparse subset, while bottom-up methods are evaluated on both sparse and full data, leaving the central comparison asymmetric. The justification that default limits make dense training impractical is plausible but does not replace a fair adapted baseline with increased detection caps, tiling, chunked training, or other practical strategies.

Metrics are too limited for the claims. Most headline results use AP/PQ at IoU 0.5, which the authors themselves acknowledge is lenient for crowded micrographs; the stricter PQ@90 result is mentioned only as a limitation rather than systematically reported across methods. Boundary quality and morphology-preservation metrics would be important for materials analysis.

The generative-model evaluation is weak and overclaimed. FID/style similarity and t-SNE overlap do not establish physical validity, controllability, or usefulness for scientific micrographs. The claim that synthetic data can “replace” real data is not supported, especially since real+generated improves only modestly over real-only.

The structured text annotations are generated with Gemini/GPT and then human-reviewed, but the manuscript provides no quantitative evaluation of attribute correctness, inter-rater agreement for text attributes, or analysis of ambiguous categories. Since multimodality is part of the claimed novelty, this evidence gap matters.

Several presentation and consistency issues reduce confidence: the microscope-type text says SEM is over 90%, while the shown figure appears to report 84.9%; the release links are missing; some figures/tables are hard to interpret from the manuscript text; and the method name UniAIMS is framed strongly despite being mostly engineering around Cellpose.

Overall, the work has a potentially useful dataset idea, but the current paper does not make a sufficiently reliable scientific case for acceptance because the dataset governance/release story, annotation validation, benchmark fairness, and generative-evaluation evidence are all underdeveloped.

strengths: This is a strong Datasets/Benchmarks contribution: EM3M is substantially larger and denser than prior public EM instance-segmentation datasets, with 5,091 electron micrographs and about 3M instance masks, plus structured image-level text attributes. The scale, density, and materials focus make the resource likely valuable to both computer vision and materials-science communities.

The annotation pipeline is unusually carefully described for a dataset paper, including human-in-the-loop pseudo-label refinement, peer review, expert validation, and a reliability study on 300 re-annotated images using Krippendorff's Alpha and PQ. The reported progression from pseudo-labels to peer review to final validation helps support the claim that model bias was reduced rather than merely propagated.

The benchmark is broad and useful. It compares two-stage, one-stage, query-based, and bottom-up paradigms, and the results convincingly show that dense EM segmentation stresses standard natural-image instance segmentation designs. The inclusion of mAP/PQ, qualitative examples, sparse/full splits, and external tests makes the empirical case reasonably complete.

The paper goes beyond a static dataset by releasing a tuned text-to-image diffusion model and showing that synthetic data improves downstream segmentation. The experiments with generated-data scaling, pretraining, FID/style metrics, and t-SNE analysis provide multiple forms of evidence for the utility of the generative component.

The authors are appropriately candid about remaining open problems, including the large drop under PQ@90, persistent failures on fibrous/ambiguous structures, scale variation, and the remaining gap to human agreement. This strengthens the paper rather than weakening it, since these limitations are well aligned with the benchmark's purpose.
weaknesses: The contribution is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks paper rather than primarily an algorithm paper. UniAIMS appears to be a strong engineering adaptation of Cellpose rather than a conceptually new architecture, so the paper's acceptance case rests mainly on the dataset, benchmark, and released tools. This is acceptable, but the manuscript sometimes frames UniAIMS with stronger method-like language than its novelty warrants.

The fairness and completeness of the instance segmentation benchmark are somewhat limited. Detection- and query-based methods are evaluated only on the sparse subset and mostly under default instance limits, so the paper establishes practical out-of-the-box limitations more than a fully optimized comparison. Stronger tuning of query counts, tiling, memory-efficient matching, or dense-scene adaptations could change some conclusions.

Some key dataset details remain under-specified for reproducibility and risk assessment: the exact data licenses/permissions for web-crawled and collaboration images, de-identification/IP handling, annotation-cost statistics, annotator expertise/training, and whether source/institution/material-level splits were considered. Random train/test splitting may overestimate generalization if near-duplicate acquisition conditions or material families appear in both splits.

The text-attribute annotations are useful, but their validation is less rigorous than the mask validation. The paper describes GPT/Gemini extraction, cross-checking, and human review, yet it does not provide attribute-wise accuracy, inter-rater agreement for the structured descriptions, or error analysis of ambiguous attributes such as material type, layering, or texture.

The synthetic-data story is promising but not fully transparent. It is not entirely clear how generated images receive segmentation masks for training at scale, how physically implausible recombinations are filtered or used, and whether synthetic augmentation ever harms rare categories. FID and DINO style similarity are helpful but only indirect measures of scientific/structural fidelity.

Several reported claims would benefit from more precise framing. For example, external evaluation uses only two small public datasets, and the conclusion that prior benchmarks are saturated is plausible but not definitive. Similarly, AP/PQ@0.5 may be lenient for dense microstructure analysis, and although the paper acknowledges this, the main tables still emphasize the easier threshold.
